talks.title: Subdomain Takeover
talks.teaser: Explains how dangling DNS records, including A records, enable subdomain takeovers and how to automate their detection.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how DNS records route a hostname either to another hostname (a CNAME) or to an IP address (an A record). When a cloud resource is torn down but the record pointing to it remains, the name is left dangling, and anyone who claims that resource name can take over the subdomain. The speaker notes that most guidance covers CNAMEs, while A records can be vulnerable too.

The risks covered include phishing from a trusted domain, defacement, and malware delivered under a legitimate-looking link. Cookie exposure depends on broad domain attributes, which matter most in certain single sign-on setups. Taken-over hosts that serve scripts can enable cross-site scripting, especially where a content security policy allowlists that subdomain. The fix is mainly DNS hygiene: removing records for resources you no longer own.

Open-source DNS Reaper handles CNAME detection well, but it does not cover A records. The speaker's approach compares public IP addresses in DNS against those in the cloud inventory, flagging records that point to cloud addresses the organization no longer owns. A daily job runs both checks and posts alerts to chat. Prevention includes removing DNS records before their targets, and using CAA records to restrict certificate issuance. Validating existing exposure is hard, and the speaker sees little built-in provider support.

talks.title: Come WiFind Me: WiFi and other RF Survelliance
talks.teaser: Explains how WiFi, Bluetooth and RFID signals can reveal where people are, and which common privacy beliefs hold up.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how radio signals from Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, RFID and NFC can be used to work out where people are and what they do. It starts with RF basics: lower frequencies travel farther, and NFC has a very short range, so implanted or passive tags pose little tracking risk. RFID readers in warehouses, stores, campuses and hospitals can track tagged items, and Wi-Fi positioning systems estimate device locations from signal timing and strength in retail and healthcare settings.

The middle section covers research and real cases. A study showed that radio signals passing through a wall could reveal movement and gait, and a dorm investigation filtered access point connection data to narrow down who was in a room. The speaker then examines claims that 5G and Wi-Fi cause health harm, comparing the advocacy material with FCC exposure limits. Many anti-EMF products, including shielding fabrics and pendants, are described as failing independent testing.

The closing advice is practical rather than alarmist. Access points carry location data, and phones that constantly broadcast saved networks leak identifying information. Turning off automatic Wi-Fi connections and Bluetooth when they are not needed helps, and MAC address randomisation reduces tracking but does not stop it entirely. For private messaging, the speaker recommends an end-to-end encrypted app over relying on shielding products.

talks.title: Who's Afraid of Responsible Vulnerability Disclosure?
talks.teaser: Surveys US laws, including the CFAA, that can expose good-faith security researchers to criminal and civil liability.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a disclaimer that the speaker is a lawyer but is not giving legal advice, which frames the discussion. The core question is how much legal exposure good-faith security researchers face when they look for flaws, even when their aim is to make systems safer. The speaker argues this matters for practitioners, students and anyone doing defensive research.

The middle section walks through a set of US statutes that have been used against researchers. The centerpiece is the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, the federal anti-hacking law from the 1980s, which covers accessing a computer without authorization or going beyond the access one was granted. The speaker explains that it can reach internet-connected devices in some situations, so testing hardware you do not own without permission may create liability even when nothing is damaged and no data leaves the system. The statute also lets anyone who suffered more than $5,000 in loss bring a civil suit, so criminal and civil consequences both come into play. The material draws on a 2020 guide from a Harvard clinic, which the speaker notes is somewhat dated given later court rulings.

The takeaway is that good intent does not remove legal risk. Researchers should understand these statutes before testing systems and should consult available guidance, such as materials from the Electronic Frontier Foundation, to reduce their exposure.

talks.title: Arizona Elections Security Prep
talks.teaser: Arizona election officials and their partners describe physical and cyber protections and threat sharing ahead of the 2024 general election.
talks.summary:
A panel of Arizona election officials, state and federal security staff, and a private-sector election vendor describes how they are preparing for the 2024 general election. The session opens with the legal framework behind elections in the state, where counties run their own processes under a bottom-up model. The state office explains its role: visiting all fifteen counties to share security practices, running a monthly statewide election security meeting, and acting as a liaison to law enforcement.

The discussion then turns to the threats election staff receive, including suspicious powder in the mail, bomb threats against several offices at once, and swatting. Panelists stress reporting these incidents so that the state fusion center can spot patterns across jurisdictions. The homeland security and federal representatives described cyber assessments of county election offices, shared telemetry across the state, tabletop exercises, and help for smaller jurisdictions that lack staff. Procedural controls such as seals, two-person handling, camera coverage, and livestreamed processes were presented as ways to build transparency. Social media was highlighted as both an intelligence source and a driver of physical risk.

The panel repeatedly named misinformation, deepfakes, insider risk from staff turnover, and threats to personal safety as their biggest concerns. Closing advice for attendees was to check claims against official sources, talk with election workers, and report threats. For practitioners, the useful takeaways are the value of standing relationships with local officials and the case for cross-jurisdiction information sharing.

talks.title: Cloud security for the network security engineer, or why it's all just so wrong these days
talks.teaser: Explains how cloud shared responsibility changes network security thinking and demonstrates a live cloud account compromise.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by contrasting traditional on-premises network defense with cloud security. Its central point is that in a cloud account an attacker may hold the same access the defender has, because the control plane replaces the network perimeter as the place where movement happens. The speaker argues that defenders should treat the root account as the closest thing to physical access and should protect it with multiple MFA methods, use a separate everyday user, and keep an inventory of every access key so they can be rotated quickly during an incident. Cloud activity logs are presented as the main record of actions that never cross the network.

The offensive section looks at how resources get exposed. Storage buckets, machine images and queues can be made public by mistake, and granting access to "authenticated users" in AWS covers every AWS account holder worldwide, not just the organisation's own users. Enumeration can start from predictable bucket DNS names. Access keys are described as the most valuable thing an attacker can find, since busy administrators often skip least-privilege configuration. The instance metadata service is shown as a route from an application flaw, such as command injection or a proxy misconfiguration, to credentials already present in the environment.

In the live demonstration, the speaker uses credentials taken from an instance to list buckets that appear secured in the console, then downloads files that include what looks like cardholder and administrative data, along with stored admin keys. The speaker notes that this activity happened outside the internal network, so little telemetry appeared beyond API records. The practical takeaways are to limit what instances can reach, treat long-lived keys as standing risk, and enable data event logging for storage.

talks.title: Leaving Doors Unlocked With Cognito
talks.teaser: Shows how misconfigured AWS Cognito user pools and identity pools can be abused to reach AWS resources.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces AWS Cognito, the managed service that handles authentication, authorization and user management for web and mobile applications. It explains its two main parts: user pools, which hold user accounts and sign-in flows, and identity pools, which map authenticated users to AWS roles so they can reach AWS resources. The speaker notes that teams often adopt it for applications already hosted in AWS.

Next, the talk covers common misconfigurations. On user pools these include self-registration left open on a sensitive panel, user attributes that can be changed to raise a role to admin, and a client secret exposed in front-end code. On identity pools it covers unauthenticated guest access, overly broad IAM roles for signed-in users, and exposed identifiers. The demonstrations show how an attacker can use a client ID or pool ID seen in traffic or source code to register, sign in, and exchange a token for temporary AWS credentials, sometimes escalating privileges. The speaker stresses that real impact depends on the application's context.

The closing section offers defensive guidance: disable self-registration when it is not needed, make attributes immutable where they should not change, review what the application assumes about attributes, turn off guest access, apply least-privilege IAM policies, and keep configuration IDs out of client code where possible. Reference material and lab walkthroughs are pointed to for further practice, along with a note that Terraform templates would be shared for hands-on work.

talks.title: Clearing the Fog: Detection and Defense against Cloud Persistence Techniques
talks.teaser: Walks through AWS and Azure persistence mechanisms in the cloud control plane and how defenders can detect them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how an attacker who already has a foothold in a cloud account keeps access over time, instead of running quick, noisy jobs. The focus is on control plane persistence in AWS, with Azure shown as a rough equivalent. Host-level tricks are set aside, and initial access is treated as a given, whether through an exposed instance, leaked keys, or a hijacked session.

The session moves from simple to advanced methods. Basic options include creating users, attaching policies or group membership, adding console logins to service accounts that only used API keys, and generating new access keys. Trust policies that let an outside account assume a role are another route, and Azure guest invitations serve a similar purpose. More involved examples cover launching an instance with an attacker-held SSH key and an added role, and a Lambda function that fires whenever a new role is created and grants the attacker's identity trust automatically. A Lambda function URL can then act as a simple command channel that lists users or creates keys on request.

For detection, the speaker maps each technique to its specific API events, noting that the same calls are also the permissions an attacker needs. Calls made from Lambda carry a recognizable user agent, and hunting depends on knowing what normal activity looks like in each environment. Takeaways include narrowing policies to the exact actions and resources needed, reviewing last-used data to trim excess access, and treating newer instance metadata protections as only partial coverage.

talks.title: Veilid, the future of privacy- aka- how to destroy capitalism with the Cult of the Dead Cow
talks.teaser: Presents Veilid, an open-source peer-to-peer framework for private messaging and decentralized apps.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Veilid, an open-source, peer-to-peer networking framework built by the Cult of the Dead Cow, with VeilidChat as its flagship messaging app. The speakers argue that people's online activity is increasingly collected and sold, and that privacy should be as easy to adopt as signing up for a mainstream service. Veilid is described as conceptually similar to combining an overlay network with Tor, designed for nodes that come and go and that switch between cellular and Wi-Fi, running on desktop, mobile and in-browser platforms.

The middle covers the design at a high level: private routing through chosen nodes, a distributed hash table with schema-based mutable records and publish-subscribe notifications, and inbound relaying so browsers can receive connections. VeilidChat's sign-up needs no phone number or contact access, and contacts are added through out-of-band invitations, with identity keys, offline recovery and duress passwords. Community projects include a VPN-style tunnel, a netcat-style tunnel tool and a game engine plugin. The project treats security as a priority: researchers' exploit code is published in the repository, and network-level pressure pushes operators to upgrade.

The closing part invites participation: a Discord community of roughly 3,000 members, ongoing documentation work, and a nonprofit foundation that supports the project and may later help judge privacy claims in apps. The main takeaway for practitioners is a model that builds privacy into the network itself rather than relying on paid servers, with an open call for contributions from non-specialists as well as engineers.

talks.title: Building a More Private Future
talks.teaser: Argues that pervasive surveillance shifts power and shapes behavior, then offers practical privacy steps for builders and users.
talks.summary:
Naomi Brockwell opens her CactusCon 2024 keynote by using Orwell's 1984 as a lens on modern life. She argues that pervasive surveillance is now ordinary rather than dramatic: phones, smart speakers, cars, doorbell cameras and data brokers gather constant streams of personal data, and governments draw on much of it through programs revealed by the Snowden disclosures and mandatory financial reporting. She frames the stakes around two risks: power shifting toward centralized companies and states, and the chilling effect monitoring has on speech, dissent and personal growth, since digital records outlast the laws and norms they were created under.

The middle of the talk looks at authoritarian examples and at how quickly freedoms were lost in past crises, then turns to what builders can do. She recommends collecting less data, protecting what is kept with strict access limits and encryption, and following research into homomorphic encryption. She also urges companies to write clear privacy policies and developers to support open-source privacy tools.

In the closing question-and-answer section she offers individual steps: move email and calendars to end-to-end encrypted services, use Signal rather than SMS, choose privacy-focused browsers, and set message expiry. Her takeaway is that privacy should be the default, and that small changes within one's own network can spread.

talks.title: Worst of Cybersecurity Reporting
talks.teaser: Roasts 2023 security articles on phones, surveillance and hyped threats, and what readers should actually worry about.
talks.summary:
Two tech reporters, Yael Grauer and David Huerta, return for their fifth annual roast of cybersecurity journalism, this time limited to print articles about privacy and surveillance. They open with a "best smartphones" piece that mixed marketing claims with no clear methodology, which made it hard to tell what was actually being compared.

The middle of the session moves through a range of stories. A security researcher's personal app choices were presented as general advice, ignoring different threat models. A cryptographic attack on SSH affected only a handful of unusual implementations but was framed as broadly alarming. Juice jacking has stayed a proof of concept for years, and a Flipper Zero article claimed intelligence agencies feared a power grid attack without much evidence. A Canadian espionage story leaned on claims without supporting detail, and a Gmail verified-badge article put the burden on users rather than the vendor. The burner phone guide missed identifiers such as the IMEI and recommended a six-digit passcode that forensic tools can crack.

The closing advice is practical: add context, treat single sources and police claims with skepticism, put missing evidence high in a story, and avoid blaming users for flaws companies should fix. For researchers, the speakers suggest explaining the real conditions behind a proof of concept, since a working demo is not the same as a practical attack.

talks.title: Unlocking RFID Security: A Deep Dive into Flipper Zero and the Vulnerabilities of Multiclass
talks.teaser: Shows how HID iClass multiclass readers can be downgraded to weaker low-frequency cards using a Flipper Zero.
talks.summary:
The talk examines HID's iClass family of RFID access control, which moved from basic low-frequency cards through iClass Elite to iClass SE. The speakers walk through how each generation handles keys and authentication, and how weaknesses in the older designs, including research published in the "Heart of Darkness" paper, carried into systems still in use. Many installations also keep older card formats active for compatibility, which matters later in the talk.

The core demonstration is a downgrade attack. Multiclass readers authenticate every card type in much the same way, so a card can be presented in its weakest format. Using Unleashed firmware on a Flipper Zero, the serial number and facility code can be captured and the credential recast as a 26-bit low-frequency card, where the facility code can be brute forced. For Elite readers, responses captured from the reader can be used to recover the site's high-security key. For SE cards, the secure access module keeps the keys out of reach, but a key set that has leaked can still decrypt the identity object and reissue the access payload as a standard Pico Pass card. The speakers stress that tooling now makes these steps simple enough that the deep hardware knowledge once required is no longer needed.

The takeaways are that the access control payload is the main thing readers verify, that facility codes and card numbers offer little protection on their own, and that mixed-mode deployments drag the whole system down to its weakest format. Suggested mitigations include using only readers that run the standard key set two, checking the vendor spreadsheet to confirm which key set each reader uses, layering controls such as guards or multi-factor checks, training staff to watch for suspicious scanning, and using RFID-blocking sleeves.

talks.title: A cactus coup at the goldrush saloon: swindling machine learning caches via wagon train
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers can hide malware in machine learning models shared on Hugging Face and run it inside ML environments.
talks.summary:
Adrian Wood and Mary Walker present a red team view of machine learning models as a software supply chain attack vector. They explain why ML environments are attractive targets: they hold large volumes of business data, rarely run endpoint detection, and their daily activity looks routine. The talk covers how look-alike organisation names on a public model repository can be claimed, and how a model file can carry code that runs whenever the model loads while its predictions stay accurate.

The middle section walks through building such a model with a Keras Lambda layer that fetches and runs a second-stage implant, and how saving the model under a different file format can get around recent restrictions. Once inside, the presenters describe common findings in shared notebooks, such as exposed API keys for data warehouses, and tools for mapping MLOps services and altering model behaviour. Mary then describes a research project that assessed thousands of model files on Hugging Face, finding very little embedded code and only one sample of actual malware, and how the code layers were extracted and disassembled.

The closing part covers defence: scanning models at ingestion, YARA rules over extracted code, H5 viewers for forensics, and the need for incident responders to learn what normal looks like in ML environments. Sandboxing at scale is judged impractical, so behavioural analysis of suspect models is suggested instead. The speakers note that the offensive code is already published, with defensive code to follow.

talks.title: The Best Free Resources to Get Started in Incident Response
talks.teaser: Points newcomers to free resources covering IR preparation, telemetry, forensic artifacts, free tools and building labs.
